title: Build a Fan Page with AI
objective: Learn to direct AI as a creative partner — brainstorming, prompting, and debugging — while building a fan page in Web Lab 2 and picking up the web languages that let you say exactly what you mean.

checklist.label: Page has a title and a main header
At least three sections of real content
Custom colors or fonts applied with CSS

panels.caption: In this tutorial, AI will help you brainstorm, code, and learn while you build your very own fan page.

steps.title: A few questions first
steps.description: Diagnostic inputs that tune the rest of the experience: workspace preference, prior web experience, and how the student has used AI before. No wrong answers, nothing graded.

questions.prompt: How do you like to work?
How experienced are you with web code like HTML, CSS, or JavaScript?
How have you used AI? Check all that apply.

steps.title: AI as a brainstorm partner
steps.description: Walk the student through forming a vision for their page, one question at a time. These answers become the project vision the AI build partner uses for every generation in this lesson.

questions.prompt: This is a website for fans of…
questions.placeholder: A band, a game, a team, a show — anything with fans.

options.label: Beginners trying to get into it

questions.prompt: People will view this page to…
questions.placeholder: Learn something? Feel the hype? Find each other?

questions.prompt: If AI helps you brainstorm ideas, are they still your own ideas? Why or why not?

steps.title: Try it out!
presetPrompts: Create a fan page with a bold header, a short introduction written for people new to the topic, and a section listing three reasons fans love it. Use a color scheme that fits the topic's vibe.
steps.description: The student picks one of the premade prompts and watches the AI build from it, using the vision they developed while brainstorming. The two prompts differ on purpose — one is bare, one is detailed — so the student sees firsthand how specificity changes the result. There is no right choice: sometimes you want AI to just give it a go. Encourage them to try both and compare.

steps.title: Rate the AI
steps.description: The student evaluates the AI's output and thinks about how they would prompt differently. Their answers inform which mini lesson gets suggested next.

questions.prompt: How would you write your prompt to get closer to what you imagined?

steps.title: Learn the language!
steps.description: Learning the language of the web gives you the words to say exactly what you mean. Each mini lesson is a small but impactful bite; the student can take as many as they like and return here after each. One choice may be highlighted as a suggestion based on the student's experience and ratings, but all are always available.

questions.prompt: What do you want to be able to say exactly?

options.label: What will it say? — HTML text

steps.title: What will it say?
steps.description: One small bite: the words on a page live inside elements, and editing them is the fastest way to make a page yours. Show the student the text in the sandbox, have them change what it says, then send them back to the hub.

starterFiles.index.html:
This page says whatever you want

Change this sentence to something only you would write.

steps.title: What goes where?
steps.description: One small bite: tags name the pieces of a page — headings, paragraphs, lists — and their order is the page's structure. Have the student rearrange or add an element, then send them back to the hub.

starterFiles.index.html:
Big heading

Smaller heading

A paragraph.

  • A list item
  • Another one

steps.title: What's the style?
steps.description: One small bite: CSS rules pick an element and describe how it should look. Have the student change a value in the existing rule and see the page respond, then send them back to the hub.

starterFiles.index.html:
Try changing my color

The rules in style.css decide how this page looks.

steps.title: What has motion?
steps.description: One small bite: JavaScript makes a page react. The sandbox has a button that changes the heading when clicked. Have the student change what the click does — different text, different color — then send them back to the hub.

starterFiles.index.html: Nothing has happened yet

steps.title: Build with your own prompts
steps.description: Now the student writes their own prompts to keep building their page. Guide them one step at a time toward the items on the website checklist — suggest the next unchecked item, help them phrase a prompt for it or code it by hand, and celebrate each item that gets done.

steps.title: Sidequest: fix it!
steps.description: A debugging sidequest on a broken page, separate from the student's project. Three planted issues range in difficulty: (1) the second paragraph's closing tag is missing, so text runs together; (2) style.css misspells 'color' as 'colr', so the heading isn't blue; (3) script.js targets the id 'buton' which doesn't exist, so the button does nothing. The student can ask AI for help fixing them — which issue they attack first, how many attempts they take, and how effective their prompts are is exactly what we want to observe. Can they fix all three?
steps.successCriteria: At least one of the three planted bugs is verifiably fixed. Celebrate if all three are.

starterFiles.index.html:
This heading should be blue

This paragraph is fine.

This paragraph never ends…

…and this one got swallowed by it.

questions.prompt: How do you learn when AI does a lot of the hard work?

steps.title: Finish it up
steps.description: Guide the student to finish the remaining checklist items on their fan page — prompting the AI, coding by hand, or both. When the checklist is done, offer extensions: another section, a second page, something animated.
steps.successCriteria: Every item on the lesson checklist is present on the student's page.
